NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF PHARMACY: Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences Dept.
Minor in Cannabis Studies: The proposed interdisciplinary minor in cannabis studies will build on the online certificate in cannabis studies by including courses in business, plant sciences, chemistry, psychology, and pharmaceutical sciences.
Business and cultivation have been identified by the certificate students as areas they would like to see the curriculum expand.
In addition, several of the URI students who have expressed interest in the program are majoring in these related fields.
Students completing the minor will demonstrate an interdisciplinary understanding of the cannabis industry from plant to market.

Specifically, students will be able to: 1) identify and evaluate sources of evidence-based information to make informed decisions related to cannabis production and therapeutics, 2) conceptually design reliable and safe cannabis products within the framework of an existing regulatory environment, and 3) apply knowledge of the bioactivity of cannabis to effectively assess treatment options and guide product development.
The minor will consist of four core cannabis specific courses.
These courses will develop core competencies in cannabis regulations, natural product separation and analysis, safe product development and manufacturing, and the evaluation of the therapeutic potential of cannabis.
The remaining credits needed to complete the minor will come from several relevant courses in pharmaceutical science, plant sciences, chemistry, psychology, and business.
Students will be able to decide which areas are most applicable to their learning goals.

Throughout the core courses, the students will be working on a threaded assignment synthesizing the concepts in each course together and culminating with the real-world experience of researching, designing, and evaluating, in concept, a cannabis product.
The discussions and practice will be hypothetical.
At no point in the program will students have direct contact with any federally illegal cannabis products or derivatives.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
The Criminology and Criminal Justice Program requests a change in organizational status from a Program to a Department.
We request this change in organizational status to achieve two goals: 1) align with current disciplinary standards within the College of Arts and Sciences and 2) position the Criminology and Criminal Justice to better achieve a fully actualized and efficient alignment with the University of Rhode Island’s Strategic Plan (2016-2021).

Background of Criminology and Criminal Justice at URI: In 2006, due to requests from the URI administration to develop programs that would attract incoming students, the Department of Sociology and Anthropology launched a specialized major in Criminology and Criminal Justice (CCJ) under the banner of a specialized “Sociology Bachelor of Science” (Sociology BS) degree.
This major and degree was distinct from both a Bachelor of Arts degree in Sociology and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Anthropology but still under the overarching Sociology and Anthropology Department.
Soon thereafter, the number of students majoring in the specialized Criminology and Criminal Sociology degree surpassed the number of students majoring in both Sociology and Anthropology.
This imbalance in the number of majors understandably generat ed disparate needs within the same umbrella department.
At the same time, URI came to understand that the institution was not fully able to capitalize on the recruitment potential of the Criminology and Criminal Justice major, as students who used the “com mon application” when applying for college would not see that URI offered a specific degree in Criminology and

3 Criminal Justice if it remained housed in the Department of Sociology and Anthropology.
These concerns helped launch the Criminology and Criminal Justice Program.
In in 2016, as a result of the CCJ major’s success and the continued growth in the number of majors, Jill Doerner spearheaded the effort to successfully propose and implement CCJ as its own self -sustaining Program outside of the Departm ent of Sociology and Anthropology.
At the time the CCJ Program was proposed, the CCJ option in Sociology (BS degree) had roughly 350 majors.
In just a few short years since its launch, the CCJ Program has close to 500 majors and has been able to hire and r etain its own exceptional faculty, unaffiliated with any other discipline at URI.
The CCJ Program at URI was officially launched in 2017.
It was initially designated as a Program, which matched similar interdisciplinary Programs at the time like Gender and Women’s Studies, Africana Studies, and Film/Media.
Since 2019, the CCJ major has boasted the second highest number of majors in the College of Arts and Sciences.

The Program is staffed by three tenure-track faculty on a 3/3 teaching load, two lecturers on a 4/4 teaching load, and three affiliated faculty contribute approximately 1 course/semester to the CCJ major.
The Program shares an Administrative Assistant with the Department of Sociology and Anthropology, and that assistant splits their time equally between CCJ and Sociology/Anthropology.
Since CCJ’s approval, it has functioned like all other departments on campus, having its own budget, faculty lines (tenure-track, lecturer, per-course and jointly appointed), and Director, who fulfills all of the same obligations and responsibilities of a Department Chair.
Rationale for Change: CCJ is committed to administering rigorous undergraduate education, producing high - quality research in areas of considerable national importance, and innovation in areas t hat will raise the profile of CCJ, the College of Arts and Sciences and URI as a whole.
We contend that a change in status from Program to Department will only better enable us to continue our excellent work in these areas and will remove any unnecessary r oadblocks to our continued success that arise from our current standing as a Program.

CCJ is currently the only Program in the College of Arts and Sciences —all other academic units are designated as Departments.
In designating CCJ as a Department, URI will acknowledge that CCJ is equal in status and importance to all other Departments within the College of Arts & Sciences and at URI.
Previously, academic majors with interdisciplinary curriculums were designated as Programs rather than Departments.
Now, the College of Arts and Sciences more completely embraces its leadership and innovation with regards to majors with interdisciplinary curriculum.
In 2020, Africana Studies and Gender and Women’s Studies both successfully achieved departmental status, and in 2021 Film/Media become a department as well.
CCJ is delighted that these disciplines are now fully recognized at URI with departmental status.
Our request for departmental status updates our designation to align with new College -wide organizational logics as evidenced by these recent changes.

4 CCJ strives to be a subject-area leader at URI, and a change in organizational status from Program to Department will only enhance CCJ’s ability to more fully align with URI’s Strategic Goals (2016-2021), especially in terms of enhancing student success (Goal 1), expanding research, scholarship and creative work (Goal 2), and embracing diversity and social justice (Goal 4).
The designation of CCJ as a Program rather than Department does not provide any benefits, only impediments.
Given the background described above, students, faculty, and staff at URI sometimes continue to believe that CCJ is part of the Department of Sociology and Anthropology.
This confusion is exacerbated by the fact that a number of faculty are jointly appointed in CCJ and Sociology/Anthropology and by virtue of the two organizational units sharing an administrative assistant.

Some examples of inefficiencies presented by this perceived affiliation follow. -In our experiences as faculty, some students report thinking that they couldn’t double major in Criminology and Sociology, or could not pursue a minor in Sociology or Anthropology, because they thought all three disciplines were one in the same. -At times, students, faculty, and staff mistakenly email the Director of Criminology and Criminal Justice with questions that pertain to the Department of Sociology and Anthropology and vice versa.
Achievements of CCJ faculty are sometimes wrongfully attributed to the Department of Sociology and Anthropology and the reverse. -Processing budgetary requests and other financial matters are not infrequently impeded by the relics of CCJ being housed under of Sociology and the distinction between budgetary lines is exacerbated by having a shared administrative assistant.
It is inefficient to still have these bureaucratic processual issues persist.
Changing CCJ to its own department will help ameliorate those inefficiencies.
Moving beyond processual issues, the successes of CCJ should be properly attributed to CCJ.

The heart and soul of the CCJ major are three junior faculty who were hired at URI starting in 2017.
These faculty should be appropriately credited within their own discipline and organizational unit at URI.
The CCJ faculty should benefit from being identified and recognized as members of a valued academic department and discipline in the University.
In terms of the CCJ faculty’s professional development and growth, this is a particularly opportune moment for CCJ to be granted departmental status and to distinguish itself as an independent academic unit.
For example, two of CCJ’s three tenure -track faculty will be seeking promotion to Associate during the 2022 -2023 academic year.
These faculty are eager to increase their service contributions to the larger University Commun ity after earning tenure, which will increase CCJ’s recognition across the larger URI community.
This increased visibility on campus should clearly signal that CCJ is an independent academic unit with unique skills to offer our community.
In addition, In F all 2022, CCJ will welcome a Distinguished Multicultural Postdoctoral Fellow.

The CCJ Fellow will join two other Fellows in this inaugural cohort, who will be affiliated with the Sociology and Anthropology Department at URI.
CCJ’s Post-Doctoral Fellow shou ld be able to

5 benefit from the same benefits that will be afforded to her peers in the cohort who are affiliated with a department rather than a program.
Criminology and Criminal Justice is an active participant in the success of students in the College of Arts and Sciences and the University as a whole.
In addition to serving approximately 500 majors, CCJ also oversees the Justice, Law and Society minor, which provides an important focus in these areas for many more students on campus.
CCJ plays a critical role in attracting students to URI and has a commitment to continued diversification of our faculty and students.
CCJ was fortunate to receive one of three Distinguished Multicultural Postdoctoral Fellow positions which will further support our involvement in diversity and inclusion initiatives on campus.
The granting of department status, and the recognition that comes with it, will only continue to strengthen CCJ’s presence at URI and the ability to recruit and retain the next generation of excellent students and faculty.

For example, CCJ’s current designation as a Program rather than a Department only raises questions of concern or confusion from prospective students and their parents at Welcome Days.
The designation never elicits questions of excitement.
The move to departmental status is also especially important as CCJ considers expanding its curricular offerings to include online programs at the graduate and undergraduate level.

INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1.
Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
Granting CCJ Departmental status can strengthen our ability to meet URI’s strategic goals, specifically with regards to enhancing student success (Goal 1), expanding research, scholarship and creative work (Goal 2), and embracing diversity and social justice (Goal 4).
As a Program, CCJ actively promotes student success, produces high-impact, innovative scholarship, and embraces diversity and social justice.

CCJ enhances student success by providing premier, interdisciplinary training to about 465 majors.
Our mission statement reflects our student-centered approach: Our purpose is to empower our graduates to meaningfully consider, contribute to, and reimagine discourses and decisions about crime and justice.
The CCJ program does this by making intentional choices about our work and remaining committed to continual professional growth and community building.
CCJ faculty are productive, energetic scholars whose research tackles some of the most pressing issues in our country.
Our tenure-track, junior faculty are experts in crucial areas of national importance such as police accountability and legitimacy, racial inequality in law enforcement, and the intersection of health and criminal justice.
They have published in high-prestige, high-

6 quality journals and have a proven track record of securing both internal and external research funding.
The move to departmental status will only enhance the competitiveness of CCJ faculty as they continue to pursue external funding.
Conferring CCJ departmental status will confer its faculty the subject-field expertise that is associated with being in an academic unit that is focused on criminology and criminal rather than in a program, which is perceived as inherently interdisciplinary.
CCJ may embrace interdisciplinarity in its approach to curriculum, but its tenure-track faculty are primarily scholars in the fields of criminology and criminal justice and their primary academic affiliation should clearly reflect that expertise when they pursue funding opportunities.
This is especially important as URI works to pursue R1 status in the coming years.
Our Program prioritizes diversity and inclusion efforts as part of its primary goals.
With approximately 30% of our majors identifying as Black, Latino, Multi-racial, Native, Asian, or non-specified, we strive to be leaders in retaining and supporting our majors from underrepresented racial groups.

Many of our faculty participate in professional development workshops and trainings around JEDI, serve on committees that specifically promote more diverse and equitable representation in higher education, and teach classes squarely focused on issues of structural inequality.
Granting CCJ Departmental status can only enhance our ability to pursue activities in support of URI’s Strategic Plan with regards to issues of innovative scholarship, student success.
Our current designation as a Program does not bestow any benefits– in fact, at times it is detrimental.
For example, candidates who were interviewed for the Multicultural Postdoctoral Fellowship often asked about our designation as a Program rather than Department, with some specifically stating that our designation as a Program raised questions about the longevity of the position and their potential path towards tenure.
The designation of the CCJ faculty as members of a Department rather than a Program will help their disciplinary colleagues immediately understand their position in academia and increase the perceived legitimacy of the URI CCJ organizational unit.

Finally, designating CCJ as a Department will help finally and more completely designate CCJ as a distinct and autonomous discipline and unit.
Since the CCJ Program was borne out of the Sociology and Anthropology Department, sometimes people at URI or bureaucratic processes within URI continue to assume that CCJ is a part of the Sociology and Anthropology Department.
This has not only been a problem in terms of CCJ’s ability to assert its own disciplinary identity, it also has resulted in inaccurate record keeping for FTE and mistakes in allocation of resources that required time and energy to correct.
In order to align with URI goals of streamlining processes to improve effectiveness, attract the best students and faculty, and better promote our excellent scholarship and pedagogy, a change in status is needed. 2.

Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
CCJ becoming a Department does not impact other units at URI.

As discussed above, CCJ has operated as a self-sustaining unit since it began and has not relied on other units for support or funding.
Given its interdisciplinary nature, CCJ has collaborated closely with other academic units on campus to offer our curriculum and create multidisciplinary experiences for our majors.

7 If granted Department status, CCJ will continue existing collaborations and seek additional opportunities across campus/disciplines.
Data on the CCJ major demonstrate its sustained success.
Since 2019 (just two years after its launch), the CCJ major has the second highest number of students in the College of Arts and Sciences, with a 3-year average of 465 majors.
We have three tenure-track faculty on a 3/3 load, two lecturers on a 4/4, and three affiliated faculty contribute ~1 course/semester to the CCJ major.
The student to faculty ratio is 17.7:1, which is in line with the College of Arts and Sciences overall student to faculty ratio (17.5:1).
The tenure track credit hour/FTE is 361, which is about 50 hours more than the College overall.
The proposed departmental status can only help CCJ to grow the efficiency of the major.
CCJ has conferred with the various departments that contribute electives to the CCJ curriculum and has received letters of support from all academic units.
There have been no concerns raised by this status change and there are no anticipated impacts on other academic units.
